screens.title: PCR and Gel Electrophoresis
screens.html:
PCR and Gel Electrophoresis

DNA Amplification and Profiling in Modern Biology

screens.title: The Biological Blueprint
screens.html:
🔑

The Biological Blueprint

If you found a single drop of blood at a scene, how could you identify the person it belongs to when the DNA sample is so tiny?

Today, we explore how scientists amplify trace amounts of DNA into millions of copies and then visualise them to solve mysteries.

Key point

PCR acts like a biological photocopier, while gel electrophoresis is our sorting machine.

screens.title: Recap: Molecular Scissors
screens.html:
QUICK REVIEW

Recap: Molecular Scissors

Before we build new DNA, let's remember how we cut and paste it. Restriction enzymes (endonucleases) recognise specific sequences called recognition sites.

Sticky Ends: Overhanging staggered cuts.

Blunt Ends: Straight vertical cuts.

screens.title: The PCR Machine
screens.html:
🧠

The PCR Machine

The Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is an in vitro (outside the body) technique used to amplify specific segments of DNA.

To make this work, we need a Thermal Cycler. This machine rapidly changes temperature to facilitate different chemical reactions.

Remember

PCR doesn't copy the whole genome—it copies a specific target sequence.

screens.title: Ingredients for PCR
screens.html:
Ingredients for PCR

To perform PCR, we must combine several key ingredients in a master mix:

Target DNA The template sequence to copy.

DNA Primers Short sequences marking the start point.

dNTPs Nucleotides (A, T, C, G) for building new strands.

Taq Polymerase Heat-stable enzyme that builds DNA.

screens.title: PCR PHASE
screens.html:
PCR PHASE

Step 1: Denaturation

The mixture is heated to 94–96°C.

High heat breaks the hydrogen bonds between the nitrogenous bases, causing the double-stranded DNA to separate into two single strands.

screens.title: PCR PHASE
screens.html:
PCR PHASE

Step 2: Annealing

The temperature is lowered to 50–60°C.

This allows DNA primers to bind (anneal) to their complementary sequences on the single-stranded template DNA. This provides a starting point for the polymerase.

screens.title: PCR PHASE
screens.html:
PCR PHASE

Step 3: Extension

The temperature is raised to 72°C, the optimal temperature for Taq Polymerase.

Taq Polymerase moves along the strand, adding free dNTPs to the 3' end of the primers to create a new complementary DNA strand.

screens.title: Why Taq Polymerase?
screens.html:
Why Taq Polymerase?

PCR requires frequent heating to 95°C. Most human enzymes, like our own DNA polymerase, would denature (lose shape and function) at this temperature.

Thermus aquaticus (Taq) is a bacterium found in hot springs. Its enzymes are heat-stable, allowing PCR to repeat cycles without adding fresh enzyme each time.

screens.title: Exponential Growth
screens.html:
🤯

Exponential Growth

After each cycle, the number of DNA copies doubles.

Cycle 1: 2 copies

Cycle 2: 4 copies

Cycle 5: 32 copies

Cycle 30: Over 1 billion copies

Fun fact

In just a few hours, PCR can produce millions of copies from a single DNA molecule.

screens.title: Gel Electrophoresis
screens.html:
Gel Electrophoresis

Now that we have plenty of DNA, we need to separate the fragments to analyse them. This is done via Gel Electrophoresis.

DNA fragments are loaded into a porous agarose gel submerged in a buffer solution within an electric field.

screens.title: PHYSICS OF BIOLOGY
screens.html:
PHYSICS OF BIOLOGY

The Charge of DNA

DNA molecules have a negative charge because of their phosphate groups.

When a current is applied, DNA is repelled by the negative terminal and moves through the gel towards the positive electrode.

screens.title: Sieving by Size
screens.html:
🔑

Sieving by Size

The agarose gel acts like a sieve.

Small fragments move through the pores easily and travel further.

Large fragments get tangled in the gel and move more slowly, staying closer to the wells.

Key point

Distance travelled is inversely proportional to fragment size (measured in base pairs, bp).

screens.title: Interpreting the Gel
screens.html:
⚠️

Interpreting the Gel

Since DNA is invisible, we use a dye that fluoresces under UV light to reveal DNA bands.

DNA Ladder

A reference sample with known sizes used to estimate unknown fragment lengths.

The Samples

Each band contains millions of identical DNA fragments of a specific length.

Watch out

One band is a 'pile' of many molecules, not a single one.

screens.title: DNA Profiling
screens.html:
DNA Profiling

DNA profiling (fingerprinting) targets Short Tandem Repeats (STRs). These are non-coding regions of DNA where a sequence (e.g., GATA) repeats.

The number of repeats varies between individuals. By comparing STRs across different loci, we can identify people with near-certainty.

screens.title: APPLICATION
screens.html:
APPLICATION

Forensic Analysis

In forensics, a DNA profile from a crime scene is compared to suspects.

For a match, every single band in the suspect's profile must align perfectly with the crime scene sample's bands.

screens.title: Inheritance Matching
screens.html:
Inheritance Matching

In a paternity test, a child must share every single DNA band with their father.

👍​

TRUE

👎​

FALSE

Now it's time to explain why...

screens.title: Inheritance Matching
screens.html:
Inheritance Matching

In a paternity test, a child must share every single DNA band with their father.

👎​

Why is that?

a) A child inherits half their DNA from their mother and half from their father, so only some bands will match each parent.

b) Children develop entirely new DNA sequences that do not relate to their parents' bands.

Answers on the next slide...

screens.title: Ethical Considerations
screens.html:
Ethical Considerations

As technology advances, we must consider the ethical implications of DNA profiling. Who owns your genetic information? How should databases be managed?

screens.title: The Ethical Debate
screens.html:
The Ethical Debate

Concerns

Privacy: Misuse of genetic data by employers or insurance.

Consent: Storing DNA from people never convicted.

Equality: Potential for racial profiling in databases.

Benefits

Exoneration: Freeing innocent people from prison.

Identification: Matching remains in disasters.

Prevention: High chance of capture deters crime.

screens.title: The Ethics of DNA Storage
screens.html:
The Ethics of DNA Storage

Should the police be allowed to keep the DNA profiles of everyone, even those found innocent of a crime, to help solve future cold cases?

screens.title: The Ethics of DNA Storage
screens.html:
The Ethics of DNA Storage

You might have said...

Arguments for: Increases the chance of solving serious crimes; ensures justice for victims long after the event.

Arguments against: Invasion of privacy; risk of data breaches; 'guilty until proven innocent' philosophy.

✅​

screens.title: Summary & Next Steps
screens.html:
Summary & Next Steps

Today we've mastered:

How PCR amplifies DNA using heat and Taq Polymerase.

How Gel Electrophoresis sorts DNA by size using electricity.

How profiling solves forensic and paternity mysteries.

Next lesson, we look at how these tools are used to create recombinant DNA for medicine.

questions.title: Written practice
questions.prompt: Explain the three main stages of a PCR cycle and why repeated cycles increase the amount of target DNA.
steps: Denaturation separates the two DNA strands by heating.
Annealing allows primers to bind to complementary sequences flanking the target.
Extension uses a thermostable DNA polymerase to add nucleotides; repeated cycles copy new templates and amplify the target.

o: Double-stranded DNA separates into single strands
DNA fragments are sorted by a gel
bank.why: Heating disrupts hydrogen bonding so the DNA strands separate.

bank.q: Why is a thermostable DNA polymerase useful in PCR?
o: It remains functional through repeated heating cycles
It makes RNA instead of DNA
bank.why: A thermostable enzyme withstands high temperatures used repeatedly during PCR.

bank.q: How do smaller DNA fragments usually move in agarose gel electrophoresis?
o: Further through the gel in a given time
More slowly than all larger fragments
bank.why: DNA is negatively charged and moves toward the positive electrode; smaller fragments usually travel further.
